findings.capability_at_risk: A naive 'trim everything over 600 chars' pass would strip the trigger vocabulary that makes the estate's long-tail skills findable at all — the exact capability the lens is meant to protect.

findings.title: The grounding pack's own byte-verification fact is REFUTED and would ban a correct recipe

findings.evidence: The grounding pack states: "On Windows, git archive and git show colon-path return CRLF worktree bytes; only git ls-files -s plus git cat-file -p gives the stored blob." The `git show` half is false. Measured (same run as F1): `git show <rev>:<path>` = 24400 B / **0 CRLF**, byte-identical to `git cat-file -p`; only `git archive` returned CRLF. This CONFIRMS windows-shell.md §8b's table (which records git show = git cat-file = 3737 B / 0 CRLF) and REFUTES the pack. Per fan-out-contract rule 4 I used a mechanically different measurement, not a re-run of the tagged probe: different repo, different file, different commit, and an in-process Python `tarfile` + `subprocess` arg-list instead of a shell `tar` pipeline. Consequence if uncorrected: an author trusting the pack needlessly bans a correct simpler recipe, and worse, may "correct" windows-shell.md §8b to match — re-introducing the exact wrong table that §8b warns about in its own words ("a rule that tells you to verify against the wrong bytes is worse than no rule: it manufactures false confidence"). EXACT EDIT — in the pack, replace that sentence with: "On Windows `git archive` returns CRLF worktree bytes; `git show <rev>:<path>` and `git cat-file -p <rev>:<path>` both return the LF stored blob (measured 2026-08-12, LF-normalisation control = 1 distinct content)."

findings.title: Missing the single highest-measured skill lever: query-specific refinement before execution
findings.targets: new skill (proposed: refining-retrieved-skills); adjacent to prompt-optimizer, continuous-learning-v2, skill-scout
findings.evidence: arXiv 2604.04323 (FETCHED, https://arxiv.org/html/2604.04323v1) measures a 6-rung ladder on Claude Opus 4.6: curated+forced-load 55.4% → curated 51.2% → curated+4 distractors 43.5% → retrieved-top5-from-34k+curated 40.1% → retrieved-without-curated 38.4% → no-skill baseline 35.4%. Qwen3.5-397B fell BELOW its own no-skill baseline (19.7% vs 20.5%), i.e. irrelevant listed skills actively mislead. Their fix — 'query-specific refinement': the agent reads the task plus all retrieved skills, tracks which parts help vs mislead, reflects, then COMPOSES a new task-tailored skill from the pieces — recovered 40.1%→48.2%, and on Terminal-Bench 2.0 lifted Opus 4.6 from 57.7%→65.5%. Crucially it is 'a multiplier on existing skill quality rather than a generator of new knowledge' (LLM-judge coverage ≥3.83 where refinement worked, ≤3.49 where it failed) — which favours this fleet's hand-authored skills. Fleet check before calling it a gap: I read the heads of the three nearest skills — prompt-optimizer ('match ECC components … Advisory role only — never executes'), skill-scout ('Search existing local, marketplace, GitHub, and web skill sources BEFORE creating a new skill'), continuous-learning-v2 (post-hoc instinct→skill evolution). All three are select-or-author flows; none composes retrieved skills into a task-tailored artifact at query time. Nothing in the 328 does.
findings.confidence: External numbers almost-certain (90-99%, fetched and tabulated). That the effect transfers to THIS fleet: likely (55-80%) — the paper's pool is 34,198 scraped skills vs 328 owner-authored, so coverage quality is probably higher here and the ceiling correspondingly lower.

findings.unverified: UNVERIFIED that a 328-description always-on listing behaves like the paper's 'curated + distractors' arm (which lost 7.7pp from just FOUR distractors) rather than its 'curated' arm. Settling experiment: take 10 tasks the fleet actually fails, run three arms at fixed model and 3 seeds — full 328-skill listing / a 20-skill hand-picked subset / no skills — and compare pass rates.
